Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this proposed bill of rights this evening I should like to express my congratulations to the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) who gave us a splendid explanation of this measure this afternoon when we first started this debate. I must confess that I spent considerable time yesterday afternoon and last night reading the various things that have already been said here in this house.
In speaking to this motion about human rights I find that this subject has been the source of long debate in years gone by. I find that similar motions have been sponsored by our own Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on more than one occasion. I find also that the sponsor of this resolution, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), supported proposed bills of rights on former occasions when they were before the house. I find also, by reading back issues of Hansard, that our Prime Minister, then the hon. member for Lake Centre, first brought to the attention of this house the need for a bill of rights on March 7, 1946, in the form of an amendment to the citizenship bill that was before the house at that time. Throughout subsequent sessions this subject has been repeatedly brought forward.
In one previous debate on this measure, on December 4, 1951, at page 1561 of Hansard, our present Prime Minister gave another very effective speech on the need for a bill

of rights. The minister of justice at that time, Mr. Garson, made a statement on the same issue and said:
If, as he contends,-
Referring to the present Prime Minister. -the law of Canada is at present defective in the matter of protecting human rights and fundamental freedoms, what is required is something which he himself has advocated on a number of occasions- a bill of rights.
I find also that on March 24, 1952 a considerable debate took place again on a proposed bill of human rights, and quite a number of members from all parties took part. Again our present Prime Minister led off in the debate, and I should like to quote some parts of his speech which I believe will be of great interest, not only to myself but to all new members in the house. On page 715 of Hansard for March 24, 1952, I find this:
I am not going to review in detail the historical development within our country of the concept of freedom. It is represented by those great charters- Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights, the Petition of Right, Habeas Corpus, and the Quebec Act and the British North America Act, peculiar to our country; and by the Statute of Westminster, whereby all dominions of the British commonwealth became equals with the United Kingdom.
Then, he goes on to say:
The quest for freedom and the desire to maintain freedom and to assure freedom is not the monopoly of any political party-and it is in that spirit I speak.
Then, he goes on to describe the contents of the bill of human rights as passed by the United Nations at San Francisco and subscribed to by the government of Canada. There is no doubt that we in Canada enjoy a true sense of liberty that is unequalled in any part of the world. This makes it imperative that all our freedoms be preserved.
Farther on in this address I found a few lines that explained the fundamentals of just what this bill meant to us, and I quote again from page 720:
Someone may ask what a bill of rights would do. A bill of rights would deny the right of any majority to interfere with my serving God as my conscience demands. It would deny the right of any government to interfere with my right to speak or write so long as I did so within the law. It would deny discrimination against any person because of his race or colour.
Farther down, he said:
A bill of rights would re-define the landmarks of liberty, which are almost erased as a result of the pathways of war becoming the permanent highroads of peace. It would give positive evidence that when Canada, at the United Nations assembly two years ago, accepted the universal declaration of human rights, that acceptance was a dedication of the Canadian people not only internationally but nationally as well. It would make parliament more careful before passing laws that would have the effect of suspending or interfering with freedom. It would mobilize the spiritual things of life

without which neither nations nor men can live a full and abundant life. Above everything else, it would make Canadians freedom conscious. As Canadians we pride ourselves on our Canadianism and how full, ample and free we are. Why is it that Canadians have not been given the equality with British subjects in the United Kingdom, in relation to actions against the crown in the courts of law? The time has come to raise the right of Canadian citizenship, and to place Canadians on equal footing with the Queen in courts of law, with the right to take any proceeding against the crown without consent of the crown, other than proceedings in respect of the armed forces, or under the Post Office Act.
Several other hon. members spoke that day in favour of this bill, including the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar who is sponsoring this present bill today. Some spoke against it, as is always the case. It seemed that the chief criticism of this bill was the infringing on rights of provincial and municipal governments. I was quite intrigued by one hon. member's objection in that while he wanted all the freedom possible for the press with which he was closely associated, he wanted the radio and the C.B.C. to be very closely censored as to what they broadcast.
I was interested to read the text of the resolution passed by the United Nations, so I procured a copy of it from the library. I should like to thank publicly the staff of the library for the fine help and co-operation which they always so cheerfully give to the members of this house. I presume that the preamble to this declaration has been quoted often in this house but it is so important that I feel it would do no harm to have it on record once again. The declaration to which we as Canadian people subscribed and which was passed by the United Nations reads as follows:
Whereas recognition of the inherent dignity and of the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world,
Whereas disregard and contempt for human rights have resulted in barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind, and the advent of a world in which human beings shall enjoy freedom of speech and belief and freedom from fear and want has been proclaimed as the highest aspiration of the common people,
Whereas it is essential, if man is not to be compelled to have recourse, as a last resort, to rebellion against tyranny and oppression, that human rights should be protected by the rule of law,
Whereas it is essential to promote the development of friendly relations among nations,
Whereas the peoples of the United Nations have in the charter reaffirmed their faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person and in the equal rights of men and women and have determined to promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom,
Whereas member states have pledged themselves to achieve, in co-operation with the United Nations, the promotion of universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms,
Human Rights
Whereas a common understanding of these rights and freedoms is of the greatest importance for the full realization of this pledge,
Now therefore
The General Assembly Proclaims
This universal declaration of human rights as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations, to the end that every individual and every organ of society, keeping this declaration constantly in mind, shall strive by teaching and education to promote respect for these rights and freedoms and by progressive measures, national and international, to secure their universal and effective recognition and observance, both among the peoples of member states themselves and among the peoples of territories under their jurisdiction.
The declaration has some thirty articles in it for the full context but it has been summarized very well in the bill by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I should like to comment on some of the paragraphs in this bill. We in this country have the widest latitude possible in freedom of speech. In fact, I do not believe there are any objections to people holding forth on whatever views they have so long as it is not advocating the overthrow of our democratic government or libelling some other person. I believe this is as it should be. They tell me that in London, England, in Hyde Park, you can walk around and hear numerous speakers talk on practically every subject imaginable and that also they have the protection of the police from being molested while doing so. This gives the individual a chance to let off pent-up feelings. If he has listeners, that is all well and good. If not, he can soon shut up and go home, but at least he has had the opportunity to voice his ideas to the general public.
Freedom of the press is another privilege which we have and which we should cherish and jealously guard. When I mention the press, I mean any means of giving or distributing news to the general public. I believe the general public are well aware that the press should have access to the news in order to distribute it to the people. This was amply demonstrated, in my opinion, by the people of London, Ontario when, even after a judge had ruled that certain civic information could be withheld from the press, the electors defeated the sitting mayor who supported this way of doing things, I understand, and withheld the information, and returned a man who advocated free access to civic information as the people's right.
This curbing of our right sometimes creeps in in the censorship of books and articles that are considered by certain individuals to be unfit for Canadians to read. In my opinion, this matter needs very careful consideration because what offends one does not offend another. No true free Canadian likes to feel that somebody has the right to say "You shall read this" or "You shall not read that". I believe that the curbing of obscene books and

Human Rights
literature lies right in our own hands. If the public would not buy them, the books would soon be off the stands and out of the stores. But it seems that the best way to promote the sale of this trash is for the announcement to be made that it is banned and is unfit to read. When this happens the sales soon soar. We know there are numbers of books that we as parents do not want our children to read. If the parents take an interest in their children's reading habits I believe this could be avoided.
Freedom of religion is another right that has been fought for over a long period of years. I believe that nothing touches a person quicker than to try to force him or her to change his or her religion. We in Canada are supposed to have this freedom, the right to worship whom we please and in whatever way we please. We do not have the violent open opposition that some denominations have had to endure but it shows up in some sections of our country in more subtle ways. While we all do not think alike along this line and while we have different ideas as to the right way to worship, we should respect the other person's point of view and they should not be denied their right to worship in their own way.
I believe, in looking back over history, that it has been the persecution endured by the different denominations which has made them strong and great. We have only to read of these persecutions to see how strong they have become today. One denomination about which I know a great deal has grown to international proportions in the last 75 years and that is the Salvation Army. That organization endured terrific violence and punishment when it first started, not only from lay people but from churchmen as well. This aroused the sympathies of some and the manner and loyalty of the followers in the Salvation Army to the ideals to which they subscribe have built them to the place which they hold today as an international organization.
We could also read, and I personally know, of some Baptist missionaries who endured very great hardships in promoting what they felt to be their right to worship. There is another denomination or sect which has endured persecution in recent times and that is the Jehovah's Witnesses. They are still persecuted in certain places today and it is for that reason, in my opinion, that they are growing as fast as they are. I read an article in the press not too long ago in which the writer claimed this sect was growing faster and making more converts than any other church group today. I am not a member of the Jehovah's Witnesses nor am I in sympathy with some of

their methods or beliefs but, in my opinion, it is just a case of history repeating itself. To persecute is to make strong.
Let us give each individual the right to worship as he pleases without any fear of persecution.
Sometimes we read of the rights of people being trampled upon then their being summarily arrested or held without communication with the outside world. This happened in Toronto not long ago. The police entered a private home without a warrant; they broke into a home in dead of night upsetting the occupants. I believe the authorities cannot be too careful in such cases to preserve the rights of the people.
There are many other rights that we as Canadians enjoy and which we must hold very dear; the right to work anywhere we can obtain employment and not to be in a position where we cannot leave a job and seek employment elsewhere; the right of the employer, which I believe should be in effect the same right, that is to employ whomever he sees fit. I believe the employers are more interested in a person's ability to do an honest day's work for an honest day's pay than in his colour or the nationality of that person.
There are other aspects of this bill which we could discuss tonight but I am sure that we as true Canadians and citizens of a country composed of many different nationalities are concerned with only one high ideal and that is to protect our freedom and to respect each other's rights and freedoms.

I must say I approach this resolution with mixed feelings. I approve of much of it but I see its danger. I see the danger of circumscribing our liberties with pious language. That is the way to get your tail in the gate. Look at the United States amendment having to do with carrying weapons. That has been one of the curses of the United States, Mr. Speaker. One of the early amendments to the United States constitution says that every American citizen can bear weapons. What does that mean? And what has it meant? Well, I will tell you what it has meant. It has meant that they have had lawlessness and ruthlessness in that nation for many years but they cannot do away with it because it is an amendment to the constitution. Admittedly, they can license them.
In the beautiful riding from which I come we have thousands of tourists from the United states. The fellows who come up from Texas drive up in their big Lincolns. They have a six-gun mounted on the footboard. They call it a footboard. I do not know just what the term is but anyway there is a spike placed out from the footboard with a washer so many inches down. You can put the six-gun down there in such a way that you can make a quick draw. Of course our immigration officials will not allow them into the country. Most of them agree to it, but some of them say no, they will not give up their guns and they will not even come into the country because they will not 96698-185

travel without a six-gun. That is an amazing situation. It is true that in Canada it is possible to have a revolver if you can prove to the local chief of police, under the Criminal Code, that you need one, but that does not entitle you to walk down Wellington street with a gun in your hip pocket; but there is the situation. They went at it by provinces, and I think every province in Canada with the exception of Quebec-they were too old in wisdom and too smart to fool with it-went for prohibition. We did not invoke any federal legislation on this question; but what did the United States do? With a similar emotionalism but with an unwise enthusiasm they decided that they would fix the thing for all time. They passed an amendment to the constitution, the Volstead Act. Not all of you remember it because some of you were too young. It was the 19th amendment to the constitution of the United States and there was to be no liquor. What happened?
Was it not the 18th amendment?

Unfortunately they went
through that regrettable period when they developed the beer barons. What happened was that through a laborious process they changed the constitution. They had to get 75 per cent of the states to agree, and that sort of thing, and it was a very difficult thing to do. That leads me, Mr. Speaker, to say this. So far as the resolution is concerned I know the words are good.
I agree with them but we have all these things now. If we get to the place where we try to circumscribe the rights we have by words we are going to get into difficulty.
I would like to say this, Mr. Speaker. Where else in the world except under British jurisdiction can a subject invoke the sovereign? In such matters as prerogative, motion of mandamus, habeas corpus, certiorari, the subject can institute an action and it is maintained in the name of Her Majesty the Queen; John Smith, or whoever he is, versus the registrar of a court or the superintendent of brokers, or even the Attorney General of Canada himself. In no other nation can that be done.
I am in sympathy with the resolution but what I say is this. Why go to work and foul our nest with a mess of pottage? We do not need it. We have got it now. Let us not take a chance. We have inherited the best from our British institutions. We have it. Let us not make a mistake; let us not goof on the question and we could very easily. I suggest that we just string along with what we have now.
Incidentally, I am quite satisfied. I have to take cognizance of the fact that the members from the province of Quebec on both sides of the house will agree with me that it is a dangerous thing to tamper with existing institutions. I know that in the first week of the session one or two of them made rather impassioned speeches and said that they must insist upon the basic rights, religious freedom, and so forth. They have had that for two hundred years and there is no suggestion that it would be taken from them under our system. In fact, far from being taken from them, it has been extended thousands of miles because in my riding of Victoria we have two magnificent Roman Catholic institutions. The good Sisters of St. Ann have an immense convent in the city of Victoria which is the main focal point of my riding. It was instituted by them as far back as 1859. Across the street they have one of the finest hospitals in British Columbia, St. Joseph's Hospital. They have gone up the coast and have hospitals in Juneau and Skagway, Alaska. This sort of thing is done but to my mind this discussion is like flogging a dead horse. There is no question about depriving anybody of their rights. Those rights exist, always will exist, and we will fight for them if we have to.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not attempt to follow the arguments of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. Already at this session it has been demonstrated that he does not speak for his party. suggest that when he now says that it is not necessary to have a bill of rights such as my leader has proposed he is flying in the face of the record of his own Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has contended for years that Canada should have a bill of rights.
A good deal has been said today about the long struggle that many members have put forth in an effort to win a bill of rights for the people of Canada. My hon. friends on the government side of the house have sung the praises of their Prime Minister. They have been good enough to admit that my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), Senator Croll, the former member for Spadina, and others in the house have also fought across the years for the establishment in Canada of a bill of rights.
To me it is a matter of regret that the house seems to be passing up the opportunity to take a significant step in that battle this very day. I concede to every member, particularly because of the importance of the subject, the right to speak to it, but when members of the same party speak in succession one after another as they have done today it does lend credence to the suggestion that the resolution is being talked out. Many Canadians will regard this as unfortunate.
Let it be perfectly clear that if the resolution in the terms in which it is drafted is passed by the house it will not have immediate legislative effect. The passing of the resolution would merely be a declaration of the opinion of the house that consideration should be given to taking whatever steps are necessary to amend the British North America Act so as to write into it a bill of rights for all Canadians. I confess that if the resolution were passed tonight it might be a long time, even a matter of years, before its terms could be fully implemented. I agree with those on the other side of the house, such as the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquar-rie), who expressed the hope that the time will soon come when we will be able to amend our own constitution in Canada in all

respects without having to go to Westminster for an amendment to the British North America Act. It may be that it will not be until we have in Canada the power to amend our own constitution that we will write into that constitution a bill of rights.
But this house has the opportunity tonight to go on record as expressing its opinion that it should be done. That, I submit, would be a declaration that would have value in this effort that has been made across the years to win a bill of rights for Canadians. Apart from a few hon. members such as the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McPhillips), who took his seat a moment ago, there is general approval of the proposition that we should have a bill of rights. Some have suggested that it should not be in the British North America Act, that it should not be in our constitution but rather should be just a statute of the federal parliament. We take the view, and I think on reflection most hon. members will agree with us, that if a bill of rights is to have any value to Canadians as a whole it must be written somewhere in such a manner that it has a bearing on legislation that can be passed both by the parliament of Canada and by the legislatures of the various provinces.
The parliament of Canada cannot by itself pass something that has control over the rights of the provinces. It is only in something of a constitutional nature that principles can be laid down that will govern both the parliament of Canada and the legislatures of the various provinces. I believe that any who give study to the question will realize that in the end if we are going to achieve a written bill of rights, and I suggest most of us agree on the desirability of that aim, it will have to be an act of a constitutional nature. That means either an amendment to the British North America Act itself or some constitutional piece of legislation arrived at after we have established a means of amending or writing our constitution here in this country.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, all that my leader's motion calls for today is for the house to declare itself in favour of steps being taken to achieve this desirable end, and I hope that even yet the house may be willing tonight to let the motion come to a vote so that the opinion of the members of the House of Commons in this twenty-third parliament may be made a matter of record.
There is just one other point I should like to make. One does not need to add to the arguments in support of a bill of rights because they have been made and made quite well from both sides of the house. But it has been a matter of interest to note the

number of members who have done a good deal of reading in this field. But I want to suggest to hon. members that in their attempt to ascertain who was the father or stepfather or father-in-law of a bill of rights in Canada they have not gone far enough back in their reading. I suggest that for an interesting speech members might read the contribution that Senator Power made in 1919 when he was the member for Quebec South in the House of Commons during the time of the general strike in the city of Winnipeg. Back in those days and despite the sense of panic that was abroad there was at least one Liberal who called for a recognition of the rights of the working men of this country, and I pay tribute still today to Senator Power for the speech he made on that occasion in 1919.
If anyone is interested in the first time when legislation was introduced that foreshadowed the idea of a bill of rights, I suggest he should turn to Hansard of March 24, 1922. He will find that on that day my predecessor as member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, introduced two private bills. One was an amendment to the Immigration Act and the other was an amendment to the Criminal Code. In introducing these bills, Mr. Woodsworth said with respect to the first one, and a similar thought applied to the second one:
The purpose of this bill is to repeal those sections of the act, so that every man in this country, whether a Canadian by birth or one who has lived in Canada, will be assured of the right of trial by jury.
Why did Mr. Woodsworth have to introduce these two bills? He did so because in the hysteria of 1919 a Conservative government had rushed through amendments to the Immigration Act and the Criminal Code, and I believe to one other statute, which took away the opportunity of trial by jury in certain instances and made pronouncements with respect to what was defined as sedition, which were clearly against the traditions and civil liberties of this country as they were understood. Later in speaking to one of these bills Mr. Woodsworth said this as recorded at page 1388 of Hansard for May 3, 1922:
The effect of the existing amendment to the Immigration Act is really to deprive a very large section of our people of the right to trial by jury- a very serious consideration. It is unnecessary for me to review the history of the claims put forth by the British people, from the time of the Magna

Human Rights
Carta and the Bill of Rights, to the right of trial by jury. That great document-the Magna Carta -was effective in restricting the arbitrary power of kings and ministers, but we have today, in this legislation which has been placed on the statute book-
He was referring to the legislation placed on the statute book by a Conservative government.
-a reversion, if I may call it so, to the condition of affairs which prevailed before the time of the Magna Carta.
Mr. Woodsworth went on to point out that the purpose of the bills which he had introduced was to re-establish certain civil liberties, certain basic rights in this country. So Mr. Speaker, in these measures introduced by Mr. Woodsworth back in 1922 you have what might be called the forerunner of the motions that have come later calling for establishment by legislation of a bill of rights for Canadians.
We in this group welcome the debate that has taken place today. We welcome the interest that has been shown in this measure. We would have liked to have had a speech from the Prime Minister. He used to speak on this measure when he was on the opposition side of the house. He used to press the immediacy of the matter, the need for action. He complained when the Liberal government talked out his resolution, or when the Liberal government refused to refer the matter to the supreme court. He complained when a committee was set up as a means of shelving the issue. We are sorry he is not here today to make one more of those speeches urging that this resolution be passed. We believe it would be a significant milestone in the struggle for a bill of rights if the house would tonight agree to the passing of this resolution. We admit it would not have immediate legislative effect, but it would be a declaration of this parliament that a bill of rights should be written into the law of this land.

believe it is desirable that I should say a few words at this stage to indicate the attitude of the government towards this subject. I recognize at once that this is a private member's resolution. It is true that it is a resolution that has all the weight of having been introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who in addition to being an authority on parliament has the additional weight of being the leader of a party in this house. speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The government welcomes the principle behind this resolution. There should be no doubt about that, because for very obvious reasons there are, to put it at its mildest, men of influence in the government who are committed to the idea of a bill of rights. There is no backing away from the attitude of the past or from any undertaking that may have been given on this subject. But we believe that it is essential that any enactment of a bill or declaration of rights, no matter what may be the legislative form, should carry the judgment of the Canadian people as a whole and should be in a form which will be acceptable to the Canadian people.
It is obvious from what we have heard in the house today, as well as what we have heard on the subject when it has been debated inside and outside parliament in the past, that there is a very wide divergence of opinion as to how we should proceed, if we proceed at all. When I say "if we proceed at all", I am referring to the opinions of others, because there are some who think we should not proceed. There is a very wide divergence of opinion, even amongst those who believe we should proceed, as to just how it should be done.
It is obvious, therefore, that the very greatest care must be taken to ensure that any such legislative enactment shall be in a form, and of effect, which will ensure that not only does it embody those rights which Canadians wish us to preserve, but also that it does not infringe on the rights or freedoms which others hold dear. And in this field we must recognize that we are up against a question, not only of individual rights but of provincial and constitutional rights.
It was for this reason that at the very outset, immediately after the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had introduced the resolution, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker), my parliamentary assistant as Minister of Justice, made his very excellent and comprehensive as well as moving speech outlining the problems which must be faced and solved before any bill or declaration of rights can be introduced by any government that claims to be responsible

Speaker, again I wish to emphasize that we do not need to hide behind these difficulties, and we do not intend to do so. We are in favour of the principle which is sought to be carried forward by this resolution, although we have very grave misgivings as to the particular method suggested.
To the same extent, indeed even to a greater extent, as we recognize the difficulty we also recognize the desirability, I might say the essential requirement, of some such provision being enacted. The needs for a bill of rights have been outlined by many speakers in the past, and by none with more force or detail than the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). These needs have been put on Hansard on many occasions and can be found there, so I am not going to attempt to enumerate them here tonight.
But it is because we recognize the difficulties that confront us that we are now working as a government, and in the Department of Justice, as has been stated by the Prime Minister and myself, to find what is the soundest approach to this problem of putting into legislative form the delineation of the rights and freedoms that are fundamental and must be preserved in Canada.
There are two views as to how this could be done. There is the view put forward by my friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that it should be by way of amendment to the British North America Act. There is the other view that it should be simply by a federal statute, whether it be in the form of a detailed statute or merely in the form of a declaration of fundamental principles. Those are the two views-on the one hand a constitutional amendment and on the other a simple statute of this parliament.
We do not reject out of hand the idea of a constitutional amendment as suggested in this resolution. However, I suggest to my friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and to my friend the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Macdonald) that we must, especially when we are talking about freedom, recognize the fact that there is one great bastion, respect for which is essential if freedom itself is to be maintained, and that is the constitution of this country. If you take an attitude that the constitution is to be amended to this extent by this parliament whether or not the provinces consent- that the constitution can be amended and that if there is no other way of doing this thing than by a constitutional amendment with or without consent, then let us amend the constitution-I say, Mr. Speaker, that if you do that then in the name of freedom you are making an assault upon the bastion of

to me that this one is so fraught with difficulty and danger that we should have to look at other methods and solutions first.
The other approach to the question of a constitutional amendment would be one which is confined, in so far as the ability of constitutional lawyers is able to do it, to areas of the constitution which might be agreed are exclusively within federal jurisdiction, and to say that, having confined it to areas of exclusive federal authority, we do not require a conference with or consent by the provinces. But the difficulty here would be that there are still large and important areas of conflict of opinion as to what are the subjects exclusively assigned to dominion jurisdiction and what are the subjects exclusively assigned to provincial jurisdiction.
I think there is fairly general agreement that in many of those areas there is overlapping, hence there is in many areas some form of dual responsibility and it would not be possible or at the very best it would be exceedingly difficult-so exceedingly difficult that it would take the wisdom of a Solomon, and I do not think there is anyone in this house who claims that degree of wisdom, not even the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-to work out that type of amendment which would have absolute acceptance by all the people of Canada.

If the hon. gentleman will forgive me I do not wish to carry this over any longer than is necessary and I wish to make a presentation in whole of the position of the government, so perhaps he would be kind enough to defer his question until I have concluded.
The other approach, Mr. Speaker,-and this is the approach that has been in essence advocated by the Prime Minister in all of the resolutions that he has moved in connection with this subject-is the enactment of a federal statute which would make it clear that in so far as any federal legislation is concerned there must be observed certain fundamental principles so that there will be preserved to every Canadian his fundamental rights and freedoms.
Here again there are several approaches or several methods which could be followed and several questions which arise. Should such a bill or declaration be specific in nature? That is, should it attempt to specify what are the limits in each case-the details of the limits of the freedoms and rights to be protected-or should it be simply in the form of a general declaration? Should it be introduced by the government and presented

to parliament, as it were, on our own motion or should it first of all be referred as a draft bill to the Supreme Court of Canada for the opinion of that court as to whether it lies within the federal competence to enact? Or should we alternatively simply refer to the Supreme Court of Canada the general question of how far does it lie within the competence of this parliament to introduce a bill dealing with the question of fundamental human rights and freedoms in so far as they affect freedom of speech, freedom of religion and the other subjects which are outlined in this resolution and in other resolutions which have been suggested to this parliament.
These then are the problems, Mr. Speaker, and I think it must be obvious to all hon. gentlemen that this statement of the problems as well as the statement made in more detail earlier by the hon. member for Rose-dale, indicate that it would not be the act of a responsible government to introduce legislation on this subject in a hurry as we would be doing if we introduced it at the present time. I think it will also be obvious that until these difficulties are thoroughly analysed and analysed with a care which we have not yet been in a position to devote to them we as a government should not introduce a proposal in specific form for a bill of rights.
By the same token I may say to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that we feel that at this stage we could not accept this proposal for a constitutional amendment as it is presented to us for the reasons I have attempted to outline earlier. I have said that we do not reject outright the proposal of a constitutional amendment but that we cannot accept their proposal as a feasible, practical and acceptable method at this time. We may be able to work out some such method, but for the reasons I have stated, the Prime Minister if he were here would not, and I am not going to and indeed will not state here tonight that we can accept the resolution as it is presently drawn.
However, I come back to where I began. This party which now forms the government, through its leader who is now Prime Minister and through other spokesmen, is on record in favour of, and he and other members of the party are the advocates of the principle of, a bill of rights. The Prime Minister's record in this house and his commitment to this ideal has been well and fully stated here today. It is our intention to continue to work on this problem so that at the earliest possible moment we can do it as a responsible government, we will be able to present some concrete proposal to parliament.
